summary: A 1970 note on flow control, comparing fixed allocation with demand allocation of resources between hosts. Flow control stops a sender from overwhelming a receiver.

plainLanguage.summary: If one friend talks too fast the other cannot keep up. This note compares ways of deciding how much one side may send.

questions: flow control fixed versus demand allocation
subtitle: Two approaches to preventing senders from overwhelming receivers.

tldr.problem: When data arrives at a receiver faster than it can process it, buffers overflow and messages are lost. A flow control scheme must prevent this while not wasting network capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares fixed allocation (pre-assign buffer space for each connection) with demand allocation (send only when the receiver signals readiness, using 'cease on link' commands).
tldr.outcome: Demand allocation was preferred because fixed allocation wastes buffers on idle connections and restricts bandwidth. Demand allocation uses buffers efficiently but can briefly overload buffers under extreme conditions.

facts.label: Author
facts.value: Edwin W. Meyer, Jr., MIT Project MAC

today: RFC 59 is Unknown status and has not been formally standardized. The 'cease on link' approach influenced later flow control designs, though modern protocols like TCP use more sophisticated window-based mechanisms rather than explicit cease/resume messages.

sections.title: Flow Control and Its Two Approaches
sections.content:
In networks, flow control prevents a sender from overwhelming a receiver with more data than it can handle. RFC 59 compares two schemes used in the early ARPANET.

Fixed allocation (from RFC 54) reserves a set amount of buffer space for each connection in advance. The receiver guarantees it will accept a certain amount of data, and the sender respects that limit. Demand allocation (or 'cease on link', from RFC 35) instead lets the receiver tell the sender to stop sending when its buffers are full, and to resume when they empty.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixed allocation is like buying tickets in advance: everyone knows how many seats are booked. Demand allocation is like a bouncer at the door: they let people in when there is space and stop them when it is full.

sections.title: Fixed Allocation: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.content:
Fixed allocation guarantees that an NCP (network control program, running on each host) will never receive more data than it promised to accept. This seems safe.

However, the RFC identifies six major drawbacks. First, buffer space allocated to a quiet connection sits idle 90% of the time, wasting resources; a demand scheme could handle many more console connections with the same buffers. Second, high-volume connections are restricted by their allocations, so bandwidth is wasted waiting for new allocations to arrive. Third, allocation requests create constant overhead in network messages. Fourth, allocations cannot be revoked, so an NCP cannot reduce space for a connection when network load increases. Fifth, the scheme optimizes for the rare case where many connections send large bursts simultaneously, not the common case of light load. Finally, because different machines add padding differently to messages, sending and receiving NCPs can lose synchronization about how much space has been used.
sections.plainLanguage: If you tell your friend, 'I have space for exactly 100 words a minute', and they send only 10 words most of the time, you waste 90 words of space. If everyone talks quietly, you could fit many more conversations.

sections.title: Demand Allocation: The Cease-on-Link Method
sections.content:
Under demand allocation, the receiver monitors its input queue for a connection. When the queue grows too large relative to remaining free buffer space, the NCP sends a 'cease on link' IMP message to the sender's IMP. The next message for that link still gets delivered, but a special bit in the RFNM (request for next message) acknowledgment tells the sender to stop transmitting. The sender confirms by sending a 'suspended' control message. Later, when the receiver has processed queued data and freed space, it sends a 'resume' message.

This scheme works well under normal and light loads. Under extreme overload, buffers can still fill completely if data arrives over many links at once faster than any process reads it. When this happens, the NCP stops accepting data from the IMP entirely. However, this situation is expected to happen rarely. When it does, the NCP can delete the input queue for the worst offending link, which quickly frees space. Once a few processes catch up reading, normal operation resumes.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps talking until the receiver says 'stop', and resumes when the receiver says 'go again'. If everyone's backlog suddenly clears, flow restarts. This is simpler and wastes less space.
